situation:
You are a recent graduate three months into your first salaried job, which pays $46,000 a year. You have asked a financial coach (judge) at ELMHURST CREDIT UNION to help you decide whether more education would pay for itself.

A two-year evening program in industrial maintenance costs $9,000, and graduates in your area earn roughly $6,000 more a year within twelve months. A four-year degree in your field costs $34,000 and leads to jobs paying anywhere from a little more than you make now to far more. Tuition for the evening program is paid up front, and your employer offers no reimbursement.

Enrolling in the two-year evening maintenance program would spend $9,000 of the $11,000 in savings that is also your emergency fund, leaving almost nothing set aside. Starting the four-year degree part-time would take six years and $34,000 in loans before any raise arrives. Your younger sister is counting on you to help with her tuition next fall.

The financial coach (judge) wants you to compare what each path is likely to earn, how steady the work is at each level of training, how the added income would be taxed, and what each leaves you able to put away for retirement, then recommend one. The coach (judge) will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and thank you after your presentation and questions.
